title: What is fine-tuning?
text:
What is fine-tuning?
Definition
Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained Transformer to a target task using
task-specific data.
General idea
pretrained model + task data + task head/objective →adapted model
Takeaway
Fine-tuning is not only model training; it is a full contract between tokenizer,
model, data, loss, and metric.

title: Typical fine-tuning workflow
text:
Typical fine-tuning workflow
1 Choose pretrained checkpoint and matching tokenizer/processor.
2 Define task formulation and output format.
3 Build dataset, split, collate function, padding/truncation logic.
4 Add or replace task head.
5 Choose optimization recipe.
6 Train, validate, and save best checkpoint.
7 Evaluate using task-relevant metrics.
8 Export/deploy with the same preprocessing contract.
Critical rule
Checkpoint, tokenizer, preprocessing, and model head must be consistent.

title: Dataset contract
text:
Dataset contract
A sample should contain
• raw text or already tokenized ids,
• label or target,
• optional metadata for analysis.
Recommended design
Keep raw data and labels clean; apply tokenizer consistently in preprocessing
or dataset mapping.
Takeaway
A clean dataset contract makes training, debugging, and evaluation much
easier.

title: Truncation is a modeling decision
text:
Truncation is a modeling decision
Problem
If max length is too short, important evidence may be removed.
Solutions
• Increase max length if hardware allows.
• Use sliding window for long documents.
• Use hierarchical pooling over chunks.
• Use long-context architectures when needed.
Takeaway
Truncation can become hidden label noise.

title: Optimization checklist
text:
Optimization checklist
• Optimizer: AdamW.
• Learning rate: warmup + decay.
• Regularization: dropout, weight decay, label smoothing.
• Stability: gradient clipping.
• Memory/speed: mixed precision.
• Model selection: save best checkpoint by validation metric.
Takeaway
Transformer fine-tuning is sensitive to optimization details.

Scenario
Typical LR range
Full fine-tuning BERT-like encoder
1e−5 to 5e−5
Training only classifier head
1e−4 to 1e−3
LoRA / adapter tuning
1e−4 to 3e−4
Large decoder fine-tuning
often conservative; task/hardware dependent
Rule
Large pretrained models usually need smaller learning rates than models
trained from scratch.

title: PyTorch training loop essentials
text:
PyTorch training loop essentials
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler ()
model.train ()
for batch in train_loader:
batch = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in batch.items ()}
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
with
torch.cuda.amp.autocast ():
out = model (** batch)
loss = out.loss
scaler.scale(loss).backward ()
scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
torch.nn.utils. clip_grad_norm_ (model.parameters (), 1.0)
scaler.step(optimizer)
scaler.update ()
scheduler.step ()

title: Freezing and gradual unfreezing
text:
Freezing and gradual unfreezing
Head-only training
Freeze backbone and train only task head. Useful for quick baseline.
Full fine-tuning
Unfreeze all parameters. Usually stronger but more expensive.
Gradual unfreezing
Unfreeze top layers first, then lower layers if needed.
Takeaway
Freezing controls adaptation capacity and overfitting risk.

title: Validation discipline
text:
Validation discipline
• Use validation set for model selection.
• Use test set only for final reporting.
• Save best checkpoint by validation metric.
• Track confusion matrix and error examples.
• Use the same preprocessing at validation and deployment.
Critical

title: Why PEFT?
text:
Why PEFT?
Problem
Full fine-tuning large models is expensive:
• many trainable parameters,
• high optimizer memory,
• difficult multi-task storage,
• higher risk of overfitting small datasets.
PEFT idea
Freeze most pretrained weights and train a small number of extra or low-rank
parameters.
Takeaway
PEFT makes large model adaptation cheaper.

title: LoRA: low-rank adaptation
text:
LoRA: low-rank adaptation
Original linear layer
y = Wx
LoRA update
Freeze W and train:
W ′ = W + ∆W
∆W = BA
where:
A ∈Rr×din,
B ∈Rdout×r
Takeaway
LoRA trains low-rank updates instead of the full weight matrix.

title: Quantization
text:
Quantization
Idea
Represent weights or activations with lower precision:
FP32 →FP16/BF16 →INT8 →4-bit
Benefits
• lower memory,
• faster inference on supported hardware,
• larger models fit on smaller GPUs.
Caution
Quantization may reduce quality; evaluate on the target task and language.

KV cache
Store previous keys and values:
K≤t, V≤t
At the next step, compute only the new token query/key/value.
Takeaway
KV cache is essential for efficient autoregressive inference.

text:

• Fine-tuning is a contract among tokenizer, model, data, head, loss, and
metric.
• Correct padding, truncation, and masking are essential.
• Optimization recipe matters: AdamW, warmup, clipping, mixed precision.
